claims.text: Surface chemical segregation is the primary driver of premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface segregation produces local regions of weakened bonding that lower the effective melting temperature relative to a homogeneous state.
Nominally homogeneous HEA nanoparticles inherently contain local elemental fluctuations and slight segregation at surfaces and interfaces.
Thermal pre-annealing or atomistic-simulation initialization can be used to create controlled variations in surface chemical ordering.
The comparison should use gradual temperature ramps in inert atmosphere or vacuum on nanoparticles 5–50 nm in size.
Localized chemical ordering and elemental segregation at nanoparticle surfaces mediate premelting behavior.
Surface segregation preferentially concentrates elements having lower cohesive energy or higher diffusion tendencies.
Concentration of those elements at the surface reduces local bonding strength.
Locally weakened surface regions act as nucleation sites for premelting.
The balance between enthalpic differences and configurational entropy affects the stability associated with elemental distribution.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface segregation will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than nominally homogeneous controls.
Enhanced surface segregation will produce an earlier appearance of disordered or liquid-like surface regions during heating.
The proposed mechanism should hold for HEA nanoparticles between 5 and 50 nm under controlled heating near the full melting point.
Extreme compositional deviations or particle sizes outside 5–50 nm may produce different thermal behavior.
A lack of statistically significant premelting-onset reduction or a lack of correlation between segregation and premelting would falsify the hypothesis.
